name: Stanford Prison Experiment
kicker: 1971 psychology study · Stopped early after guards turned abusive
briefing: In the summer of 1971, psychologist Philip Zimbardo turned a Stanford University basement into a fake prison and had college students play “guards” and “prisoners” for what was supposed to be two weeks. Some guards grew so harsh that the study was shut down after only six days. It became a famous lesson about how roles can change behavior, but critics later found that the researchers had coached the guards, and several guards said they were only acting, so many psychologists now doubt its conclusions.

tossups.p: An undergraduate named David Jaffe played the role of “warden” in this study, which recruited its subjects through a newspaper ad offering $15 a day. Participants were randomly assigned to be either guards or prisoners, and the “prisoners” were arrested at their homes by real Palo Alto police officers to make the setup feel believable.
tossups.r: Planned to last two weeks, this study was ended after only six days when psychologist Christina Maslach objected to what she saw. For 10 points, name this 1971 psychology study, led by Philip Zimbardo, that simulated a jail.

tossups.p: This study’s guards wore mirrored sunglasses and carried wooden clubs, while the “prisoners” wore numbered smocks and stocking caps instead of their own clothes. One guard, who took on a theatrical, harsh persona inspired by a character from the movie _Cool Hand Luke_, became known to the others as “John Wayne.”
tossups.r: The U.S. Office of Naval Research funded this study, hoping to learn why conflict breaks out in military prisons. For 10 points, name this 1971 study in which college students played guards and prisoners in a fake jail at a California university.

tossups.p: Christina Maslach, who was dating this study’s lead researcher at the time, visited the basement where it was held and was disturbed enough by the conditions to demand that it end. One participant nicknamed “the Sarge” stood out for his unusual military-style discipline.
tossups.r: Zimbardo and Maslach later married. For 10 points, name this 1971 psychological study of prison life, planned for two weeks but stopped after only six days.

tossups.p: A riot broke out among the “prisoners” in this study on its second day, and several were released early after extreme stress reactions. Philip Zimbardo later co-wrote a 1980 article on resisting mind control.
tossups.r: This study’s guards grew increasingly controlling over just six days before psychologist Christina Maslach’s objections ended it early. For 10 points, name this 1971 simulation of prison life at Stanford University.

trap.title: Stanford University or the study?
trap.body: Some real tossups ask for “Stanford University” and use this study’s own details, like the guards and prisoners, as just one clue among unrelated campus facts (the Marshmallow Test, the Stanford-Binet test) — a few even say “accept Stanford Prison Experiment” as a bonus. A tossup built entirely around guards, prisoners, Zimbardo, and Christina Maslach wants the more specific answer: the study itself.
trap.fix: If the clues wander into other Stanford trivia from a different decade or a different researcher, the answer is Stanford University. If every clue is about guards, prisoners, six days, or Zimbardo, give the specific study. If you only catch “Zimbardo experiment,” you’ll still get prompted to be more specific.
